cultural.summary: Plant a little earlier in the season to dodge the disease's favorite wet-weather window!
cultural.how: Sow around 30th May rather than late June.

details.what_it_does: Reduces disease pressure by getting the crop through its most vulnerable early growth stage before peak monsoon humidity arrives.
materials_needed: No extra materials — this is a timing change
application_steps: Check your local agricultural zone's recommended sowing window for maize.
Within that window, choose the earliest safe date — trials found disease severity lowest around 30th May and highest around 30th June.
Prepare your field and seed so you're ready to sow at this earlier date.
Sow as normal once the date arrives.
details.time_commitment: No extra time beyond normal sowing
details.frequency_detail: Once per season, at the start
details.expected_results_timeline: Preventive measure — reduced BLSB symptoms typically visible from July onward if disease pressure is present, compared to later-sown crop.

cultural.summary: Skip the extra-large nitrogen serving — a lighter, balanced meal keeps disease away!
cultural.how: Avoid high nitrogen doses; cap at the recommended rate for your zone.

details.what_it_does: Lowers plant susceptibility — high nitrogen (150 kg/ha) was directly linked to increased disease severity in field trials.
preparation_steps: Find your zone's recommended nitrogen rate for maize (ask your local KVK if unsure).
application_steps: Do not exceed the recommended rate — specifically avoid pushing toward 150 kg/ha.
Split the total nitrogen dose across 2-3 top-dressing applications rather than one large dose.
Apply at recommended growth stages: basal/at sowing, knee-high stage, and tasseling.
details.time_commitment: 30-45 minutes per application for a small plot
details.frequency_detail: 2-3 split applications across the growing season
details.expected_results_timeline: Ongoing effect through the season; disease severity difference visible by mid-to-late vegetative stage.
safety_notes: Avoid direct skin contact with concentrated urea

cultural.summary: Give your maize a raised ridge to call home — it grows happier and healthier there!
cultural.how: Sow maize on ridges rather than flat ground.

details.what_it_does: Improves drainage and airflow around the plant base, reducing the humid microclimate the fungus needs.
materials_needed: Hoe, small plough, or ridger tool
preparation_steps: Before sowing, form ridges across the field roughly 15-20cm high, adjusted for your soil type and rainfall.
Space ridges according to your normal row spacing.
application_steps: Sow seeds along the top of the ridges rather than on flat ground.
Maintain the ridges through the season — re-firm them if heavy rain washes them down.
details.time_commitment: Half a day to a full day for ridge formation on a small-to-medium plot
details.frequency_detail: Once, at field preparation, with occasional maintenance after heavy rain
details.expected_results_timeline: Drainage benefit is immediate; disease severity difference becomes visible as the season progresses.

cultural.summary: Give each plant a little extra elbow room so disease can't sneak between them!
cultural.how: Use wider spacing rather than tight spacing (avoid 60cm × 15cm).

details.what_it_does: Reduces humidity buildup between plants by improving airflow. Closer spacing (60cm × 15cm) was found to increase disease severity and reduce yield.
materials_needed: Measuring stick or rope marked at target spacing
preparation_steps: Determine your variety's recommended spacing range (seed packet or local extension office).
Choose the wider end of that range.
application_steps: Mark out rows and planting points using your measuring tool before sowing.
Sow one seed per marked point at the correct depth for your variety.
details.time_commitment: Adds roughly 10-20% more time to normal sowing, done once
details.frequency_detail: Once, at sowing
details.expected_results_timeline: Airflow benefit immediate; disease severity difference visible as season progresses.

cultural.summary: Two sneaky weeds are secretly hosting the disease — hunt them down first!
cultural.how: Prioritize removing barnyard grass and nutgrass specifically.

details.what_it_does: Removes the two specific weed species found to harbor and spread the BLSB pathogen.
materials_needed: Hand tools (khurpi/hoe) or normal weeding method
preparation_steps: Learn to identify Echinochloa colonum (barnyard grass) and Cyperus rotundus (nutgrass) — ask your local KVK for a photo reference if unsure.
application_steps: During normal weeding rounds, prioritize removing these two species completely, including root systems where possible (especially nutgrass tubers).
Remove and dispose of pulled weeds away from the field edge, not piled near the crop.
details.time_commitment: Modest extra time added to normal weeding rounds
details.frequency_detail: Ongoing throughout the season, roughly every 2-3 weeks
details.expected_results_timeline: Ongoing preventive effect; reduces pathogen reservoir over the course of the season and future seasons.

cultural.summary: Snip away the lowest leaves during rainy season to keep the humid disease hideout away!
cultural.how: Pluck the lower leaves and sheaths from each plant.

details.what_it_does: Physically removes the lowest leaves/sheaths where humidity concentrates near the soil, directly reducing the fungus's favored microclimate.
materials_needed: Hands, or a small knife/blade for tougher sheaths
preparation_steps: Wait until plants are well-established, roughly 3-4 weeks after emergence — check plant vigor before starting.
application_steps: During the rainy season, identify the lowest 1-2 leaves and their sheaths on each plant.
Gently pull or cut these lower leaves and sheaths away from the stalk, close to the point of attachment.
Dispose of removed material away from the plant base.
Repeat periodically as new lower leaves age into the 'lowest' position.
details.time_commitment: A few seconds per plant; 1-3 hours total for a small-to-medium field per pass
details.frequency_detail: Every 2-3 weeks through the rainy season
details.expected_results_timeline: Reduces humid microclimate immediately; disease severity difference builds over the rainy season.
safety_notes: Be gentle to avoid damaging the main stalk or upper healthy leaves

biological.summary: A specially selected friendly fungus strain that crushes disease growth in the lab!
biological.how: Apply Trichoderma sp. isolate MDA-1 as seed treatment and/or soil application.

details.what_it_does: Introduces a highly effective antagonistic fungus (87.1% mycelial inhibition of the pathogen in lab trials).
materials_needed: Trichoderma sp. (MDA-1 isolate or general Trichoderma product)
preparation_steps: Purchase or obtain a Trichoderma-based product from a local agri-input store or KVK.
Follow the product's label rate for seed treatment or soil application.
application_steps: Seed method: mix the product with seed in a container, ensuring even coating.
Allow treated seed to air-dry briefly in shade before sowing.
Sow treated seed as normal.
Soil method (alternative/additional): mix product into water or compost per label rate and apply to soil at the base of the planting row.
details.time_commitment: 15-30 minutes for seed treatment on a small-to-medium batch
details.frequency_detail: Once, at sowing
details.expected_results_timeline: Establishes in root zone over 1-2 weeks; protective effect builds through vegetative stage.
safety_notes: Store away from direct sunlight and extreme heat

biological.summary: Coat your seeds in a protective bio-bath before they even go in the ground!
biological.how: Treat seed with Trichoderma viridi at 20g per kg of seed.

details.what_it_does: Introduces a confirmed effective bio-agent at a specific research-validated dosage.
preparation_steps: Weigh out your seed batch.
Calculate 20 grams of Trichoderma viridi powder per kilogram of seed.
application_steps: Place seed and measured powder in a container or bag.
Mix thoroughly by shaking or hand-tossing until seed is evenly coated.
Sow immediately or within the same day for best results.
details.frequency_detail: Once, at sowing
details.expected_results_timeline: Establishment over 1-2 weeks; protective effect through vegetative stage.

biological.summary: Two friendly microbes teaming up in the soil for extra-strong protection!
biological.how: Apply Trichoderma asperellum + Bacillus subtilis, 200g/m² each, to soil before sowing.

details.what_it_does: Combined bio-agents shown in a two-season trial to reduce BLSB incidence and improve yield more than either alone.
preparation_steps: Obtain both bio-agent products from your local KVK or agri-input store.
Measure each at 200 grams per square metre of planting area, scaled to your bed's actual area.
application_steps: Mix into the soil surface at the planting row before sowing.
Work in lightly with a hand tool.
Sow seed as normal after application.
details.frequency_detail: Once, before sowing
details.expected_results_timeline: Effect builds gradually over the season; season-long protection rather than a quick fix.

biological.summary: A friendly bacteria spray that trains your plant's own immune system to fight back!
biological.how: Apply Pseudomonas strains (AS19, AS21) as foliar spray.
biological.frequency: Every 10-14 days from early vegetative stage

details.what_it_does: Triggers systemic immune response in the plant and has direct antifungal activity — pot trials showed 25-38% reduction in disease incidence.
preparation_steps: Obtain a Pseudomonas fluorescens-based product from a local agri-input source.
Mix per the product's label rate in a sprayer with clean water.
application_steps: Spray evenly over foliage, covering upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Spray in early morning or evening to reduce evaporation and improve absorption.
details.time_commitment: 20-30 minutes for a small-to-medium plot per session
details.frequency_detail: Starting at early vegetative stage, repeat every 10-14 days
details.expected_results_timeline: Systemic resistance builds over 1-2 weeks; ongoing protection maintained through repeated spraying.

botanical.summary: A strong eucalyptus leaf brew that knocked out disease growth by over 90% in the lab!
botanical.how: Spray Eucalyptus globulus aqueous leaf extract at 50% concentration.

details.what_it_does: Strong direct antifungal effect — 92.1% mycelial inhibition in lab trials, the strongest single botanical result for this disease.
preparation_steps: Collect eucalyptus leaves — pack a container half-full with crushed/chopped leaves, fill the rest with water, for roughly a 50% concentration.
Crush or roughly chop the leaves to help release compounds.
Steep for 24 hours (cold soak), or gently boil for 15-20 minutes and let cool.
Strain through a cloth or fine strainer, keeping only the liquid.
Let cool completely if boiled.
application_steps: Pour the prepared extract into your sprayer.
Spray evenly over foliage, covering upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Apply in early morning or evening.
details.time_commitment: 30-45 minutes preparation, 20-30 minutes application per session
details.frequency_detail: Every 10-14 days starting at early vegetative stage (suggested, pending direct field confirmation)
details.expected_results_timeline: Direct antifungal contact effect — some benefit within days of each application, cumulative protection over repeated sprays.
safety_notes: Wash hands after preparation and application
Prepare fresh extract each time rather than storing long-term

botanical.summary: A wild hillside weed brewed into a spray that completely stopped disease growth in the lab!
botanical.how: Spray Eupatorium adenophorum crude extract at 2.5% concentration.

details.what_it_does: Your strongest single result for this disease — 100% mycelial inhibition, matching chemical fungicide performance. Locally abundant across Himachal hillsides.
materials_needed: Fresh Eupatorium adenophorum leaves (confirm identification with KVK)
preparation_steps: Collect fresh Eupatorium adenophorum leaves — confirm identification with a knowledgeable local source before first use.
For 2.5% concentration, use roughly 25 grams of fresh crushed leaf material per litre of water.
Crush the leaves to release compounds.
Steep for 24 hours, or gently simmer 15-20 minutes and cool.
Strain thoroughly through a cloth or fine strainer.
application_steps: Pour strained extract into sprayer.
Spray evenly over foliage, upper and lower surfaces.
Apply in early morning or evening.
details.frequency_detail: Every 10-14 days
details.expected_results_timeline: Given the very strong lab inhibition rate, expect a noticeably strong direct effect; monitor after first 1-2 sprays.
safety_notes: IMPORTANT: known to be toxic to grazing livestock if consumed in quantity
Wear gloves when crushing/handling large quantities
Avoid application near grazing animals' feeding areas
Do not let livestock graze on treated plant material immediately after spraying

botanical.summary: A Persian lilac leaf extract that fights disease almost as well as the strongest options!
botanical.how: Spray Melia azedarach (Bakain) extract on foliage.

details.what_it_does: Strong antifungal effect — 87.8% mycelial inhibition in lab trials.
preparation_steps: Collect fresh Bakain leaves.
Crush the leaves.
Steep in water — roughly equal parts crushed leaf to water as a starting ratio, since exact concentration wasn't fully specified in source — 24-hour cold soak, or simmer 15-20 minutes and cool.
Strain thoroughly.
application_steps: Spray on foliage, upper and lower surfaces.
Apply in early morning or evening.
details.frequency_detail: Every 10-14 days
details.expected_results_timeline: Noticeable direct effect expected; monitor and adjust based on results.

botanical.summary: Rich worm-made compost that feeds your soil and fights disease at the same time!
botanical.how: Work vermicompost-enriched organic compost into soil at 50% concentration before sowing.

details.what_it_does: Doubles as fertility input and disease suppressant — 83.8% mycelial inhibition in lab trials, likely via improved soil microbial competition.
preparation_steps: Obtain vermicompost, purchased locally or from your own setup.
application_steps: Work vermicompost into the soil at the planting row before sowing, at roughly 50% of your total soil amendment volume.
Sow seed into the amended soil as normal.
details.frequency_detail: Once, before sowing (repeatable each season as part of normal fertility management)
details.expected_results_timeline: Ongoing benefit through the season; disease-suppressive effect builds gradually alongside fertility benefits.

local_practice.note: No HP-district-specific traditional practice found specifically for BLSB. Worth asking directly in farmer interviews.

turcicum_leaf_blight.name: Turcicum Leaf Blight (Northern Corn Leaf Blight)

cultural.summary: Grow HP-tested tough maize lines that naturally shrug off leaf blight!
cultural.how: Use resistant/tolerant genotypes identified in CSK HPKV's Palampur trials.

details.what_it_does: Uses genetics rather than intervention — CSK HPKV's Palampur trials identified specific resistant inbred lines under real Himachal field conditions.
materials_needed: Access to CSK HPKV's recommended resistant seed lines
preparation_steps: Contact CSK HPKV Palampur or your local KVK for their current publicly-released resistant maize lines.
application_steps: Source seed of the recommended resistant variety through official channels.
Sow as you would any maize variety, following that variety's specific spacing/timing recommendations.
details.time_commitment: Variable time to contact KVK/source seed (days to weeks); sowing itself is standard time
details.frequency_detail: Once, at the seed-sourcing stage each season
details.expected_results_timeline: Resistance is built in from germination — reduced disease expression visible throughout the season without additional intervention.

cultural.summary: Wider spacing and a lighter nitrogen meal both keep leaf blight pressure down!
cultural.how: Use wider spacing and avoid excess nitrogen at top-dressing.

details.what_it_does: Same underlying logic as BLSB cultural treatments — reduces disease-favorable humid, crowded conditions.
materials_needed: Same as BLSB's 'Wider Plant Spacing' and 'Reduced Nitrogen Dosing' treatments
preparation_steps: See full step-by-step under BLSB → Cultural → Wider Plant Spacing and Reduced Nitrogen Dosing
details.frequency_detail: At sowing (spacing) and split top-dressing stages (nitrogen)
details.expected_results_timeline: Same as referenced BLSB treatments

biological.summary: This friendly fungus shows up again and again in trials as a top disease fighter!
biological.how: Apply Trichoderma harzianum as seed treatment plus foliar spray during vegetative stage.
biological.frequency: Seed treatment once; foliar spray every 10-14 days

details.what_it_does: Repeatedly confirmed as one of the most effective bio-agents against this pathogen across multiple independent studies.
preparation_steps: Seed treatment: follow the same method as BLSB's Trichoderma seed treatment (product label rate, coat seed evenly, dry briefly in shade).
application_steps: Sow treated seed same day.
For foliar spray: mix product per label rate with water in sprayer.
Spray on foliage during vegetative stage, covering upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Apply in early morning or evening.
details.time_commitment: Seed treatment: 15-20 minutes once. Foliar spray: 20-30 minutes per session
details.frequency_detail: Seed treatment once at sowing; foliar spray during vegetative stage, suggest every 10-14 days
details.expected_results_timeline: Establishment over 1-2 weeks after seed treatment; ongoing protection through foliar applications.

biological.summary: Two strong bacterial allies working together to fight off leaf blight fungus!
biological.how: Apply Bacillus subtilis and Pseudomonas fluorescens as foliar spray or seed treatment.

details.what_it_does: Both bacteria independently show strong antagonistic activity against the pathogen; combined use may offer broader protection.
preparation_steps: Mix both products per their respective label rates into the same sprayer tank.
Confirm with product labels or your KVK that combining is safe for the specific products you have.
application_steps: If foliar: spray evenly over leaves in early morning or evening.
If seed treatment: follow standard seed-coating method as described for other bio-agents above.
details.frequency_detail: Suggest every 10-14 days if foliar, once if seed treatment
details.expected_results_timeline: Protection builds over 1-2 weeks and continues through repeated application.

botanical.summary: A traditional sweet flag extract that completely stopped fungus growth in the lab!
botanical.how: Spray Acorus calamus (Vacha) extract at 1% w/v concentration.

details.what_it_does: Strongest result across the entire maize research dataset — 100% mycelial inhibition.
materials_needed: Acorus calamus (Vacha/sweet flag) rhizome or leaf material
preparation_steps: Obtain Acorus calamus material — rhizome is most commonly used traditionally, though confirm which part matches the trial if possible.
For 1% w/v, use 10 grams of plant material per litre of water.
Crush or grind the plant material to increase extraction surface area.
Steep for 24 hours, or simmer gently 15-20 minutes and cool.
Strain thoroughly through a cloth or fine strainer.
application_steps: Pour into sprayer.
Spray evenly over foliage.
Apply in early morning or evening.
details.frequency_detail: Suggest every 10-14 days as a starting schedule
details.expected_results_timeline: Given the 100% lab inhibition result, expect a strong direct effect; monitor after first 1-2 applications.

botanical.summary: A strong herbal spray that knocks out three-quarters of the fungus growth!
botanical.how: Spray Artemisia indica extract at 2.5% w/v concentration.

details.what_it_does: 75.18% mycelial inhibition in lab trials.
preparation_steps: Collect fresh Artemisia indica leaves.
For 2.5% w/v, use 25 grams of leaf material per litre of water.
Crush leaves and steep — 24-hour cold soak, or 15-20 minute simmer and cool.
Strain thoroughly.
application_steps: Spray on foliage in early morning or evening.
details.frequency_detail: Every 10-14 days
details.expected_results_timeline: Strong direct effect expected given the solid lab inhibition rate; monitor and adjust.

botanical.summary: A cheerful wildflower leaf spray that fights fungus nearly as well as Artemisia!
botanical.how: Spray Lantana camara extract at 2.5% w/v concentration.

details.what_it_does: 74.00% mycelial inhibition — very close to Artemisia's performance.
preparation_steps: Collect fresh Lantana camara leaves (leaves only, not berries).
For 2.5% w/v, use 25 grams crushed leaf material per litre of water.
Crush leaves and steep — 24-hour cold soak, or 15-20 minute simmer and cool.
Strain thoroughly.
application_steps: Spray on foliage in early morning or evening.
details.frequency_detail: Every 10-14 days
details.expected_results_timeline: Similar to Artemisia — strong direct effect expected.
safety_notes: IMPORTANT: Lantana camara berries are toxic if ingested, particularly to children and livestock
Handle the whole plant with care even though only leaves are used
Keep prepared extract away from children

botanical.summary: A wild Himalayan spice plant, already growing on hillsides, that fights fungus too!
botanical.how: Spray Xanthoxylum armatum (Timru) extract at 2.5% w/v concentration.

details.what_it_does: Moderate inhibition (44.21%) — likely most useful as a supplementary treatment, from a plant already common across Himachal's mid-hill forests.
materials_needed: Fresh Xanthoxylum armatum (Timru) leaves or bark/fruit
preparation_steps: Collect fresh Timru plant material.
For 2.5% w/v, use 25 grams crushed plant material per litre of water.
Crush and steep — 24-hour cold soak, or 15-20 minute simmer and cool.
Strain thoroughly.
application_steps: Spray on foliage in early morning or evening.
details.frequency_detail: Every 10-14 days
details.expected_results_timeline: Moderate effect expected — consider combining with a stronger botanical (Vacha) or a bio-agent for best results.
safety_notes: Generally safe as a traditional food/medicine plant

botanical.summary: A strong herbal spray that performed as well as top treatments when paired with a friendly fungus seed treatment!
botanical.how: Apply Datura stramonium leaf extract at 50% concentration, combined with Trichoderma seed treatment.
botanical.frequency: Foliar spray every 10-14 days; seed treatment once

details.what_it_does: Best performing when combined with seed-stage Trichoderma — matched top treatments in a field trial.
preparation_steps: First, treat seed with Trichoderma before sowing (same method as other Trichoderma seed treatments in this document).
Separately, prepare Datura extract at 50%: pack a container about half-full with crushed Datura leaves, fill with water.
Steep 24 hours, or simmer 15-20 minutes and cool.
Strain thoroughly.
application_steps: Spray extract on foliage during the growing season.
Apply in early morning or evening.
details.time_commitment: Seed treatment: 15-20 minutes once. Foliar prep: 30-45 minutes per session; application 20-30 minutes
details.frequency_detail: Seed treatment once at sowing; foliar spray suggest every 10-14 days
details.expected_results_timeline: Combined approach builds protection from sowing through the vegetative season; expect notably better performance than either treatment alone.
safety_notes: CAUTION REQUIRED: Datura stramonium is genuinely toxic — all parts contain alkaloids poisonous if ingested
Can cause skin/eye irritation on contact for sensitive individuals
Wear gloves when handling and crushing the plant
Keep prepared extract and all plant material away from children and livestock grazing areas
Wash hands thoroughly after handling; avoid touching face/eyes during preparation
This treatment requires genuine caution, not just routine hygiene

botanical.summary: Two essential oils that completely stopped fungus growth in a recent lab study!
botanical.how: Apply Tea Tree oil and Garlic oil, conservatively diluted.
botanical.frequency: Foliar application, rate to be confirmed

details.what_it_does: Complete inhibition of the pathogen in a recent (2025) in vitro trial.
preparation_steps: Dilute both oils conservatively in water, since exact field concentration wasn't specified beyond the in vitro trial.
Small-patch test on a few plants before wider application.
application_steps: Spray on foliage after confirming no adverse reaction from patch test.
Apply in early morning or evening.
details.frequency_detail: Exact field rate not yet confirmed — monitor closely and adjust
details.expected_results_timeline: Strong effect expected given the 100% lab result, but field response should be monitored closely since this is a newer, less field-tested option.
safety_notes: Essential oils can be potent — avoid over-concentration

local_practice.note: No HP-district-specific traditional practice found specifically for turcicum leaf blight. Flagged for farmer interviews.

fall_armyworm.name: Fall Armyworm (Currently Active Outbreak in HP, ~19,000 hectares affected as of July 2026)

cultural.summary: Traditional local seeds might naturally resist this pest better than newer hybrids — worth testing!
cultural.how: Plant indigenous/desi seed varieties instead of hybrids.

details.what_it_does: A natural-farming trainer reported this pest spreads much less in indigenous seeds compared to hybrid seeds — unverified but directly relevant to your research question.
preparation_steps: Source indigenous/desi seed varieties, e.g. through local seed savers or KVK.
application_steps: Consider planting a side-by-side comparison plot: indigenous seed vs. hybrid seed under equal conditions.
Monitor both plots for fall armyworm incidence through the season.
details.time_commitment: Standard sowing time, plus ongoing monitoring time if running a comparison
details.frequency_detail: Once, at sowing
details.expected_results_timeline: Comparison results would build over the season as pest pressure develops — this is a genuine data-gathering opportunity, not a guaranteed fix.

cultural.summary: Keep an eye out for HP-tested maize lines bred to resist this exact pest!
cultural.how: Use resistant inbred lines identified in CSK HPKV's 2023 Palampur screening trial.

details.what_it_does: CSK HPKV directly screened maize lines for fall armyworm resistance alongside three fungal blights.
materials_needed: Access to CSK HPKV's resistant seed lines, once publicly released
preparation_steps: Contact CSK HPKV Palampur or local KVK to check on public release status of these specific lines.
application_steps: Sow as normal once seed is sourced.
details.frequency_detail: At sowing, pending public release of specific lines
details.expected_results_timeline: Resistance built in from germination.

local_practice.summary: Tie up your maize cobs in the kitchen where cooking smoke naturally keeps bugs away!
local_practice.how: Tie maize cobs in bundles and suspend them in the kitchen area.
local_practice.category_note: This is a post-harvest storage practice, not a field-stage pest treatment. Recommend placing in storage module.

details.what_it_does: Cooking smoke naturally deters insect pests and controls moisture in stored cobs.
materials_needed: A kitchen area with regular cooking-fire smoke exposure
preparation_steps: Harvest and dry maize cobs to appropriate storage moisture level.
application_steps: Tie maize cobs (along with pigeonpea and cowpea pods, if applicable) in bundles.
Suspend the bundles in the kitchen area where cooking smoke will regularly reach them.
Leave in place through the storage period.
details.frequency_detail: Once per harvest, maintained through the storage period
details.expected_results_timeline: Ongoing protective effect throughout storage as smoke exposure continues.
safety_notes: Standard kitchen fire safety precautions apply

cultural.summary: A balanced diet keeps stalks strong and standing tall against rot!
cultural.how: Avoid excess nitrogen combined with dense planting.

details.what_it_does: High nitrogen combined with dense planting increases stalk rot susceptibility.
materials_needed: Same as BLSB's 'Reduced Nitrogen Dosing' treatment
preparation_steps: See full step-by-step under BLSB → Cultural → Reduced Nitrogen Dosing
details.frequency_detail: At top-dressing
details.expected_results_timeline: Ongoing effect through the season.

cultural.summary: Harvest promptly once ready, don't let mature plants sit in wet fields!
cultural.how: Avoid leaving mature crop standing in wet field conditions.

details.what_it_does: Stalk rot pathogens exploit weakened, waterlogged stalks left standing too long.
preparation_steps: Monitor crop maturity closely as harvest time approaches.
application_steps: Harvest promptly once the crop reaches maturity, especially avoiding delay during wet weather.
details.time_commitment: Standard harvest time, just done promptly rather than delayed
details.frequency_detail: Once, at harvest
details.expected_results_timeline: Immediate — reduces the window for pathogen exploitation of weakened stalks.

cultural.summary: Grow HP-tested maize lines specifically bred to resist stalk rot!
cultural.how: Use resistant genotypes identified in CSK HPKV mid-hill trials.

details.what_it_does: CSK HPKV has directly evaluated maize inbreds and hybrids against bacterial stalk rot under Himachal mid-hill conditions.
materials_needed: Access to CSK HPKV's recommended resistant lines
preparation_steps: Contact CSK HPKV or local KVK for current recommended resistant lines from this research.
application_steps: Source and sow recommended seed as normal.
details.frequency_detail: At sowing
details.expected_results_timeline: Resistance built in from germination.

biological.note: No dedicated bioagent trial specific to maize stalk rot found. Trichoderma/Pseudomonas evidence from BLSB and turcicum leaf blight above plausibly cross-applies but is unconfirmed for stalk rot specifically.

botanical.note: No dedicated botanical trial specific to maize stalk rot found. Flagged as a research gap.
